evidence_quotes.quote: This study aims to understand sources of drinking water, how water is accessed by local communities, and determine the barriers associated with access to potable water and management in the rural villages of Madiba and Enqabeni.

Following this guideline, in Enqabeni which has 2,048 households, a sample of 205 households was selected whereas in Madiba with 1,307 households, a sample of 131 households was chosen (95% conﬁdence level; 5% margin of error).

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 5 (Water sources, transportation, and consumption)
evidence_quotes.quote: When asked about their main source of water, all the respondents (100%; n = 205) in Enqabeni village indicated that they obtained water from open water bodies (rivers, wetlands, streams, springs and ponds).

When an oﬃcial from the municipality was asked why communities do not have access to safe drinking water in democratic South Africa, it was indicated that budget planning and allocation of funds are not balanced by the authorities. It was stated by an oﬃcial that the municipality receives less than half of the budget requested for water and sanitation.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 9 (Corruption and mismanagement of funds)
evidence_quotes.quote: Corruption and mismanagement of funds have also emerged as challenges aﬀecting water service delivery in the study area. When respondents asked if corruption is contributing to poor water service delivery, all the respondents in Enqabeni said yes.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water service access in two rural villages (Enqabeni and Madiba) in the Eastern Cape Province, South Africa.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study touches on institutional and governance factors broadly by discussing post-apartheid constitutional/policy promises, municipal budget shortfalls for water projects, failure to build or repair village water infrastructure, and perceived municipal/traditional-leader corruption in project funds and COVID-19 rainwater tank distribution. However, under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification, Criterion 2 is NOT met because the study does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, administrative discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Instead, its empirical focus is on generic rural infrastructure non-delivery/maintenance failure, municipal capital budget constraints, project corruption, and macro-level post-apartheid governance background.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical evidence from a systematic random sample questionnaire survey of 336 rural households, semi-structured interviews with municipal officials, ward councilors, and traditional leaders, and field observations.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete household access outcomes, including 100% reliance on untreated open water bodies in Enqabeni and 70% in Madiba (with 30% using an unpumped borehole and non-functional community taps since 2016), collection distances exceeding 5 km, and supplemental weekly water-truck rationing.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households and local informants in two villages), general infrastructural/institutional barriers, access outcomes, and cross-sectional mixed-methods design are identifiable, though no rule-type legal or administrative exposure is analysed.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (survey instruments translated to IsiXhosa for fieldwork and transcribed into English).

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods case study (systematic random sample household survey, semi-structured key-informant interviews, and field observations)
population_and_sample: 336 systematically sampled rural households in Enqabeni (n = 205 of 2,048 households) and Madiba (n = 131 of 1,307 households) villages in Winnie Madikizela-Mandela Local Municipality, Alfred Nzo District Municipality, Eastern Cape Province, plus purposively sampled municipal officials, ward councilors, and traditional leaders
exposure: Historical apartheid infrastructural neglect, municipal budget shortfalls for rural water project implementation and tap/borehole maintenance, and perceived corruption/mismanagement of municipal funds and rainwater tank distribution
outcome: Household drinking-water sources (reliance on untreated open water bodies vs. unpumped community borehole or vendor water), lack of functional tap water, collection travel distance (>5 km), transport mode, and daily consumption quantity
rationale: Exclude under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this mixed-methods empirical study examines rural household drinking-water access in two South African villages (meeting c1, c3, c4, c5, c6), it fails Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope clarification. Rather than analysing a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism governing service access (e.g., eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, administrative burden, tariffs/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or regulatory/ownership structure), the paper investigates generic rural infrastructure absence and non-repair, municipal capital budget shortfalls, perceived corruption in project funds and rainwater tank distribution, and broad macro-governance background regarding the unfulfilled post-apartheid constitutional right to water.
